title: The Fer expansion of a driven spin under $\mathfrak{su}(2)$ operations cannot terminate beyond first order
abstract: The Fer expansion writes the propagator of a driven quantum system as an ordered product of exponentials, each generated by the time integral of an effective Hamiltonian that governs the evolution left over by the previous factors. It can be stopped after finitely many factors whenever this leftover evolution is known in closed form, for instance when the effective Hamiltonian commutes with itself at all times, or precesses about a fixed axis with constant angular velocity. For $\mathfrak{su}(2)$, in any representation, from a qubit to a spin of any size, we resum the Fer recursion into a closed map on curves in $\mathbb{R}^3$. We prove that, for a real-analytic drive, in both cases the expansion stops beyond the first factor only trivially, when the first exponential is already exact.

title: Single-photon time qubit: Quantum-vacuum control and complementarity of the arrow of time
abstract: Treating the arrow of time as a controllable quantum variable rather than a fixed external parameter is a central challenge in quantum physics. Recently, Bloch~\cite{Bloch2025} proposed the theoretical concept of a \emph{time qubit}, a two-level control space $\mathcal{H}_T=\mathrm{span}\{\ket{+},\ket{-}\}$ that selects between opposite Hamiltonian evolutions $\hat{H}_{\pm}=\hat{H}_0\pm\hat{V}$, but this paradigm has remained experimentally unrealized. Here we formulate the quantum-optical theory of a single-photon time qubit---uncovering quantum-vacuum control and complementarity of the arrow of time---and experimentally probe and validate its predictions using phase-resolved single-photon interferometry from two coherently seeded entangled nonlinear biphoton sources~\cite{Lee2018,Yoon2021}. First, we show theoretically and verify experimentally that a controlled $\pi$ pump--seed phase inversion during pair creation from the quantum vacuum flips the stimulated displacement generator $\hat{V}\to -\hat{V}$ on top of the spontaneous two-mode squeezing background $\hat{H}_0$, reversing the stimulated evolution time [$\hat{U}_{\mathrm{stim},-}(t)=\hat{U}_{\mathrm{stim},+}(-t)$] and enabling universal single-qubit $\mathrm{SU}(2)$ control and postselection-free first-order tomography on the temporal Bloch sphere. Second, we prove that spontaneous idler vacuum fluctuations record complete which-branch (temporal-direction) information whereas the shared coherent seed erases it without cascading or aligning the idler beams, establishing an exact wave--particle complementarity law $|\bm{r}|=\mathcal{V}=|\alpha|^2/(1+|\alpha|^2)$ for the purity of the arrow of time and enabling direct first-order measurement of the Loschmidt time-reversal echo.

title: Quantum Cryptanalysis on Two Feistel-Type Constructions
abstract: With the rapid advancement of quantum computing, the security of traditional cryptographic systems is facing significant challenges. As a fundamental component of symmetric cryptography, block ciphers have attracted increasing attention regarding their quantum security in recent years. In this paper, we propose new quantum attacks on two Feistel-type constructions, i.e., New Structure IV and the lightweight block cipher LBlock, under the quantum chosen-plaintext attack (qCPA) model. First, we construct an 8-round quantum distinguisher for New Structure IV and perform an $r(r>12)$-round quantum key-recovery attack. Compared with Li et al.'s qCPA-based result presented at INSCRYPT 2024, our attack reduces the time complexity by a factor of $2^{n/2}$, where $n$ denotes the subkey length. Second, we design a 9-round quantum distinguisher for LBlock and extend it to an $r(r>15)$-round quantum key-recovery attack. The proposed quantum distinguisher covers one more round than Liu et al.'s automated-search distinguisher at ASIACRYPT 2025, which results in a $2^{16}$ reduction in the time complexity of our $r$-round quantum key-recovery attack on LBlock. Furthermore, by analyzing the structure of the round function and the key scheduling of LBlock, we reduce the subkey guess space for the 15-round attack from 76 bits to 52 bits, lowering the time complexity from \(O(2^{38})\) to \(O(2^{26})\) by a factor of \(2^{12}\).

title: Shot Allocation Strategies in Debugging Quantum Circuits
abstract: Debugging quantum programs remains challenging due to the nature of quantum measurement. As quantum algorithms and systems scale, it is increasingly crucial to develop rigorous debugging and verification approaches. Statistical assertion-based debugging validates quantum program behavior through repeated circuit execution and statistical hypothesis testing, but existing frameworks treat shot count as a fixed input parameter, leaving the problem of optimal shot allocation across multiple mid-circuit assertions unexplored. To improve debugging efficiency by making better use of given shot counts, this paper proposes and evaluates four shot allocation strategies within the QDB quantum debugger implemented within the CUDA-Q framework. These allocation approaches: equal split, static weight allocation, adaptive entropy routing, and sequential retirement, use statistical approaches to test whether qubits have expected state characteristics at different points in execution. We evaluate these allocation strategies on different circuits, under both noise-free and depolarizing noise conditions. We show how adaptive strategies use shots efficiently by concentrating them on assertions with high uncertainty. This substantially reduces total shot usage while maintaining comparable debugging confidence.
comments: 2 pages,1 figure, IEEE Quantum Week Poster Session

title: Rényi multi-entropy of graph states and the $n -> 1$ limit
abstract: Rényi multi-entropy extends the Rényi entropy to pure states of more than two parties. It is defined by a replica contraction at integer replica number $n$, and the multi-entropy is its $n\to1$ limit. In holography this limit is conjectured to compute the area of a minimal soap-film web in the bulk. Understanding multi-entropy for general states, however, is harder. Unlike the bipartite case, the replica contraction is not a moment of a density matrix, and the continuation to $n=1$ has to be found by other means. We study this problem for qubit graph states. We show that at every odd $n$ the contraction equals $2^{-k/2}$, where $k$ is a sum of ranks of matrices over a finite field, one row and one column per qubit. We define a class of graphs that we call collision-controlled, for which the rank sum is a polynomial in $n$. This class includes graphs without even cycles and all complete bipartite graphs. The natural polynomial $n \to 1$ continuation is a finite sum over partitions of the parties. While the Rényi multi-entropy is non-increasing under single-qubit Pauli measurements at every odd integer $n>1$, the continuation to $n=1$ is not. A $Z$ measurement on one qubit of an odd ring with $2r + 1 \geq 7$ qubits raises it from $(r+1)\log 2$ to $(2r-1) \log 2$. Thus the continuation is not an entanglement monotone.
subjects: Quantum Physics (quant-ph) ; High Energy Physics - Theory (hep-th)

title: Cavity models of non-Abelian gauge theories
abstract: In quantum optics and related fields, cavity quantum electrodynamics provides a powerful framework for modeling the low-energy properties of bound charges coupled to electromagnetic fields, using a minimal set of atomic levels and isolated photonic modes. Here, we develop a similar framework for non-Abelian gauge theories, focusing on the pure-gauge dynamics of SU(2) fields as the conceptually simplest example. Starting from the corresponding Yang-Mills Lagrangian, we derive an SU(2) cavity Hamiltonian in the Coulomb gauge, represented in terms of only three localized bosonic modes. Unlike its non-interacting electromagnetic counterpart, this model exhibits a nontrivial excitation spectrum featuring bound composite gauge particles ('glueballs') as the lowest-energy configurations. We extend this framework to one-dimensional arrays of coupled SU(2) cavities and discuss the driven excitation of a glueball condensate and the clustering of multi-glueball states as two elementary interaction-induced processes in these models. These examples offer a glimpse into the multitude of novel many-body phenomena that arise within this cavity SU(2) framework and we show how this physics at the interface between particle physics and quantum optics can be experimentally explored using state-of-the-art superconducting quantum circuits.
subjects: Quantum Physics (quant-ph) ; High Energy Physics - Lattice (hep-lat)

title: CO$Φ$ - COmpiling PHotonics into dIgital quantum circuits
abstract: Photonic and qubit-based (digital) approaches to quantum computing are largely regarded as separate paradigms. This article aims to bridge these paradigms by developing a method for mapping quantum-optical systems onto qubit-based quantum circuits. The key ingredient enabling this mapping is the introduction of a truncation of the Fock space describing single-mode optical states. Within this framework, representations of basic photonic operations are developed, including the phase-rotation operator, the displacement operator, the squeezing operator, and the beam splitter. Explicit quantum circuit constructions are provided for Fock-space truncations of dimension $N=2$ and $N=4$. We discuss benchmarking of the implemented operations and identify the regime of applicability and the limitations of the proposed method. The presented results can be used to simulate quantum optical circuits on qubit-based quantum computers, with special relevance to Gaussian Boson Sampling in the low-photon-number regime. To demonstrate the practical applicability of this approach, we complement the theoretical framework with a Python-based quantum programming tool CO$\Phi$ that compiles Blackbird quantum-optics programs into qubit-based OpenQASM circuits using a truncated Fock-space encoding. The compiler is available on GitHub at this https URL .
comments: 38 pages, 16 figures, GitHub repository: this https URL

title: Bidirectional Path Integral Monte Carlo Simulation of Quantum Circuits
abstract: We propose an approximate classical algorithm for estimating quantum circuits' transition amplitudes, $\langle \Psi_f | \hat{U} | \Psi_0 \rangle$, based on Monte Carlo sums over bidirectionally sampled Feynman paths. The algorithm generates Feynman paths, i.e., sequences of intermediate computational basis states, by combining information from random walks initiated at both the input and output states, $\Psi_0$ and $\Psi_f$, respectively. It further combines this bidirectional approach with Multiple Importance Sampling, a powerful variance reduction technique that avoids variance peaks caused by divisions by the very low sampling probabilities associated with hard to reach paths. Empirical data demonstrate the superior convergence rate exhibited by the bidirectional algorithm over a unidirectional, forward-only sampling approach. This superiority is due to the effectiveness of the proposed algorithm in finding and weighting paths with non-zero amplitude in an extremely sparse path space. Sum of paths algorithms exhibit very favourable space complexity. Monte Carlo replaces exhaustive enumeration of the exponentially large path space by stochastic sampling, the computational cost being determined by the variance of the estimator. This work demonstrates these two features by presenting results on very large quantum circuits, with up to 4096 qubits.

title: Collision-aware Bayesian mitigation of photon loss in linear optical quantum circuits
abstract: Photon loss is the dominant noise source in linear optical quantum circuits. Each lost photon turns an ideal n-photon outcome into a pattern with fewer photons, so the detector counts no longer follow the ideal output distribution, and the lossless events that do follow it become exponentially rare as the photon number grows. Discarding the lossy events (postselection) therefore wastes most of the data at realistic loss rates, and the ideal distribution has to be inferred from the lossy counts themselves. Recycling-based mitigation (Mills & Mezher, Quantum 2026; Quandela's photon_recycling) reweights lossy samples to recover lossless probabilities, but its estimators are biased and restricted to the no-collision sector, where each output mode holds at most one photon. We instead treat the raw counts as Multinomial observations under per-photon binomial loss and infer the ideal output distribution and the loss rate jointly from a Bayesian posterior, which extends naturally to outputs with collisions. On data from the independent Perceval simulator at the scale of prior work (n=4 photons in m=20 and m=10 modes), the posterior has lower KL divergence than both recycling and postselection at every tested loss rate in the no-collision benchmark. In the collision regime it recovers the loss rate and the collision-pattern probabilities, which recycling cannot estimate, and stays below recycling at every loss rate and below postselection except at low loss, where the two are comparable. Its advantage over recycling grows with the sample count, and it supplies credible intervals that the baselines lack.

title: NeST: ultra-high-rate qLDPC codes with sub-$50μ$s stabiliser cycles via spin shuttling
abstract: Quantum low-density parity-check codes now reach encoding rates up to 50% at useful distances. Their checks however are long-range group actions, not local neighbourhoods, and that connectivity has so far been supplied by neutral atoms. Silicon spin qubits offer the same primitive --- coherent transport of qubit blocks --- through electron shuttling, and on microsecond rather than millisecond timescales. They however travel along fabricated tracks rather than free space: permutations an atom array obtains by moving tweezers must here become collision-free motions on a physical lattice. We here present the first code and spin-qubit hardware co-design. We build an architecture whose geometry mimics that of a family of non-abelian groups, broad enough to host codes of excellent parameters: a hierarchy of nested conveyor-belt loops on a plain square lattice of shuttling tracks, in which every group multiplication becomes a rigid, globally controlled motion of whole qubit trains. We call it NeST, for Nested Shuttling Tracks. A code search over the family returns rate-20% mitten codes up to $[[1400,280,\leq 28]]$, and circuit-level simulations including shuttling dephasing give thresholds above $10^{-3}$ with sub-$50\mu$s stabiliser cycles, two to three orders of magnitude faster than neutral-atom implementations. Via extrapolations, we estimate that this largest code may reach a logical error probability per qubit per round of $10^{-14}$, assuming a ten-fold improvement on early shuttling demonstrations, with other physical errors at p=0.1%. Logic is compatible with NeST too: for the [[150,30,10]] code we build a code-surgery gadget in which every qubit again moves only by rigid belt motions, at no qubit cost and a 29% increase in gate layers. This demonstrates that ultra-low-overhead fault tolerance and a fast clock speed are not competing goals, and that silicon spin qubits can supply both.

title: Optimal Quantum-Circuit Synthesis and Implementation of General Unitaries with Parallelized Bitstring-Conditioned Rotations
author_note: Showing the first 3 and last 3 of 10 authors
abstract: We theoretically introduce a quantum-circuit synthesis protocol to realize any $n$-qubit transformation $U\in U(2^n)$, up to a diagonal. The resulting circuit is directly native to and optimal in gate count and depth for systems where bitstring-conditioned rotations with tunable angle and axis, $C^{(n-1)}R(\theta,\phi)$, form the set of native operations. Subsequently, we suggest how this protocol can be implemented in a few-mode superconducting circuit, and experimentally demonstrate the method for the smallest nontrivial case, i.e., for two qubits. We report an average gate fidelity of 97.6 % for Haar-random two-qubit unitaries up to phase shifts in the computational basis. Importantly, these results suggest that multimode devices, such as those in the multimon or multiunimon families may become competitive with qubit-array networks for general-unitary implementations for qubit counts as low as three.

title: Controlled-Z Gates via Floquet Coupling to Two Auxiliary States in Transmon Circuits
abstract: High-fidelity entangling gates are essential for quantum information processing. In transmon circuits, higher excited states provide additional pathways for engineering interactions within the computational subspace. Here we demonstrate controlled-Z (CZ) gates that exploit two noncomputational states, $\ket{02}$ and $\ket{20}$, through selective Floquet coupling. The nontrivial parametric modulation can activate both auxiliary transitions from $\ket{11}$ while suppressing the leading exchange between $\ket{01}$ and $\ket{10}$. Based on this approach, we develop two gate protocols: a nonadiabatic round trip through a bright auxiliary superposition and adiabatic evolution along a zero-energy dark state, both achieving average gate fidelities above $99.99\%$ in numerical simulations. Control of the modulation phase further extends the bright-state protocol to conventional and unconventional geometric CZ gates. Effective-model simulations show that unconventional control improves tolerance to residual $ZZ$ coupling and static qubit-frequency offsets relative to conventional control over the parameter ranges examined. Simulations including neighboring spectator qubits show that the original nonadiabatic bright-state and adiabatic dark-state CZ protocols retain high gate fidelities. This framework offers new routes toward the experimental realization of CZ gates and their geometric implementations.

title: Multimode Parametric Amplifier for K-Band Quantum Measurements
abstract: We demonstrate K-band nondegenerate three-wave-mixing amplification in a multimode resonator comprising an array of 500 SNAILs. Pairing K-band signal modes with lower-frequency internal idler modes enables 20 dB of gain continuously from 19.6 to 25.6 GHz with pump frequencies below 32.2 GHz. At 20 dB gain, the 3-dB bandwidth ranges from 2.6 to 11.7 MHz, and the input-referred 1-dB compression power reaches -100.9 dBm. In the 20-22 GHz band, the average added noise is 0.73 quanta. A two-mode nondegenerate parametric amplification model describes the measured gain response and gain-bandwidth behavior, while a multimode Kerr model captures the overall compression scale. Our amplifier provides a practical solution for implementing a state-of-the-art readout of superconducting qubits in the K-band.
comments: 6 pages, 4 figures; 3 pages of supplementary material

title: Active isolation of transmon readout with a tunable inductive bridge
author_note: Showing the first 3 and last 3 of 8 authors
abstract: Scalable superconducting quantum computation requires fast, high-fidelity readout. Currently, this is assisted through cryogenic amplification of the readout signal. In traditional dispersive readout schemes, the amplifiers that are used to provide high signal-to-noise ratio also generate thermal noise that can decohere the qubits, demanding additional ferrite-based isolators to suppress this noise. Here, we integrate a chip-scale microwave switch, the tunable inductive bridge, into the readout chain of a fixed-frequency transmon. Flux-pulsing the switch, such that it transmits only during the readout, did not make a discernable difference to qubit coherence, residual excited-state population, or readout fidelity metrics. By injecting broadband noise that mimics amplifier thermal photons, we show that the switch suppresses the resulting qubit dephasing by more than $30$~dB, consistent with its independently measured on-off ratio, establishing it as a potential chip-based integrated replacement for readout-chain isolators.

title: Finite-size spin fluctuations and fixed-index sweeps in a ferromagnetic spinor condensate
abstract: We find a dip in the optimized rotation quantum Fisher information of a zero-magnetization ferromagnetic spin-1 Bose-Einstein condensate near the excited-state quantum phase transition. Its displacement from $\epsilon_c=-q$ decreases on an inverse-size scale. At $q=0.6,0.8,1.0,1.2$, the dip value of $F_{\max}$ equals $2\langle S^2\rangle$ for $N$ up to $3840$, linking it to total-spin fluctuations. A semiclassical orbit average normalized by the classical density of states describes the dip over $N=120$--$3840$ with maximum relative residual below $0.028$; a small power law fits comparably. Inserting the measured energy offsets directly into the semiclassical formula leaves residuals of $17$--$30\%$, so $\kappa$ acts as an effective cutoff. Among retained states, spin-nematic squeezing occurs at the spectral edges. Separately, fixed-index excited-state sweeps have half-excitation times between $11.2$ and $13.1$ times their ground-state counterparts, with local size exponents increasing across the four sizes.

title: A high-speed, large-aperture 3D printed laser shutter for cold atom experiments
abstract: Cold atom experiments require optical shutters with rapid and repeatable actuation. Existing solutions often involve high cost, limited aperture diameter and slow transitioning. We present a 3D-printable shutter design featuring a large aperture of 4.5 mm diameter, low-cost assembly, and robust performance. The device achieves switching times of $399\pm8~\mu$s with delays of $2.7\pm0.2$ ms for a fully illuminated aperture, with four different shutters demonstrating repeatable performance. We measure the shutter speed to be $7.0\pm0.1$ m/s. This approach offers an accessible, scalable solution for cold atom and other optical experiments requiring multiple shutters with precise light control and avoids the need to resize or precision-align a beam through an aperture.
comments: 6 pages, 6 figures, 1 table. The data and models, including experimental data, CAD files, a parts list, assembly instructions and thermal and electrical models that support the findings of this study are openly available in UQ eSpace at this https URL

title: Achieving ultrahigh-temperature superfluidity in atomic Fermi gases by suppressing pairing fluctuations
abstract: Achieving room-temperature superconductivity has been a long-sought goal of both the physics community and the industry. The superfluid transition temperature $T_\mathrm{c}$ of a Fermi system initially increases with increasing pairing strength between fermions following the mean-field prediction of the Bardeen-Cooper-Schrieffer (BCS) theory, and is then suppressed by pairing fluctuations as the strength increases further, which prevents $T_\mathrm{c}$ from becoming high. Here we propose a mechanism for suppressing pairing fluctuations using the synergy between population imbalance and momentum space confinement in lattice systems, enabling an ultrahigh $T_\mathrm{c}$ at moderately strong attraction. We show that in a three-dimensional optical lattice, strong Pauli exclusion between paired and excess majority fermions pushes up the pair excitation energy and suppresses finite-momentum pairing fluctuations. The mechanism is general to any lattice with a finite Brillouin zone; the optimal imbalance is modest ($p\lesssim 0.1$), keeping the Zeeman field small and avoiding orbital complications. The gapped pair dispersion at moderate imbalance exponentially suppresses thermal condensate depletion, providing a testable signature. The gapped dispersion, enhanced condensate fraction, and pseudogap reduction are all accessible in present-day experiments. This work opens new avenues toward room-temperature superconductivity.

title: Efficient Ground-State Manifold Amplification for Rydberg Atom Arrays via Houdayer Cluster Updates
abstract: We demonstrate a hybrid quantum-classical approach for exploring ground-state manifolds of maximum independent set problems, in which quantum hardware supplies the initial solutions and an entirely classical post-processing algorithm expands them, increasing the solution diversity of quantum hardware measurements by up to several orders of magnitude. Quantum optimization devices, while capable of generating high-quality solutions, can suffer from fundamental sampling limitations. This is particularly problematic for applications that strongly depend on a large variety of uncorrelated optimal solutions. We apply the Houdayer cluster update algorithm to systematically expand quantum-generated solution sets through classical post-processing. We validate our approach on a test bed of 43 problem instances from QuEra's Aquila analog annealing device, achieving diversity amplification factors, defined as the increase in the number of distinct solutions at a given set size, of up to 11923x with a median of 24.3x across different problem scales and hardness parameters. Because exact ground-state degeneracies are known for these instances, the recovered fraction of the manifold can be measured rather than bounded: post-processing recovers a median of 21% of the ground-state manifold, and provably all of it for six instances. We also demonstrate that, in some cases, the classical post-processing can discover independent sets larger than those found by the quantum hardware, thus improving on solution quality and not just diversity. While the method is non-ergodic and cannot guarantee complete manifold coverage, it consistently discovers a larger number of high-quality, and in some cases strictly better, configurations than quantum sampling alone. This work demonstrates how simple classical post-processing can enhance the utility of quantum optimization results.
subjects: Quantum Physics (quant-ph) ; Disordered Systems and Neural Networks (cond-mat.dis-nn); Quantum Gases (cond-mat.quant-gas); Optimization and Control (math.OC)

title: Tuning between collective dynamics and scrambling through initial-state symmetry alignment in long-range spin models
abstract: Long-range interactions in many-body quantum systems give rise to a wide range of dynamical phenomena, from collective dynamics well described by integrable mean-field models with symmetric all-to-all couplings, to fast scrambling of quantum information from disordered long-range interactions. Here, we investigate scenarios in which both regimes emerge within a single deterministic, translation-invariant XY spin model with long-range couplings. We consider a sparse powers-of-two (PWR2) graph, where each spin interacts with a logarithmic number of neighbors, and a power-law-decaying model. By altering the initial state via local perturbations on a completely symmetric state, we show that the dynamics changes from collective to scrambling as witnessed by bipartite and multipartite entanglement measures. We characterize this collective-to-scrambling crossover using Lyapunov exponents in the semiclassical regime, and show that the spectral properties of the coupling graph adjacency matrix provide a very efficient tool to predict the onset of fast scrambling. Our results offer a unified framework for controlling the switch between collective and scrambling dynamics in a setup accessible in experiments with neutral atoms in cavities or in tweezer arrays.
comments: 20 pages, 11 figures in the main text, and 6 figures in the appendices

title: Systematic Truncated Wigner Approximation for Open Spin Systems Reveals Long-Range Order Far from Equilibrium
abstract: Long-range interactions can protect dissipative order against fluctuations, but determining when they do so in two dimensions remains out of reach for existing many-body methods. We develop a continuous SU(2)-covariant truncated-Wigner framework that maps the problem onto stochastic dynamics with one Bloch sphere per site. Derived systematically from the exact Stratonovich-Weyl evolution of the Lindblad equation, it generates both drift and reservoir noise for arbitrary spin $S$. Benchmarks against exact and tensor-network calculations validate its description of non-equilibrium dynamics and steady states. Applied to 400-site two-dimensional dissipative anisotropic XY lattices, our method reveals physics missed by mean-field and perturbative approaches: vortex-antivortex proliferation destroys the predicted staggered-XY phase for nearest-neighbour coupling, whereas algebraically decaying interactions stabilize an extended $\mathbb{Z}_2$-ordered phase. We obtain the first beyond-mean-field steady-state phase diagram of the long-range interacting model, revealing reentrant loss of order at strong coupling and closure of the ordered region beyond $\alpha\approx 3.5$. Our new method provides a scalable route to strongly correlated driven-dissipative systems with long-range interactions, higher-dimensional geometries, spin-boson couplings, and spins beyond one half, relevant to modern experiments with magnetic atoms and polar molecules in optical lattices and tweezer arrays.

title: Fully Automated Wannier Disentanglement via Projectability Selection in Gaussian and Augmented Plane-Wave Frameworks
abstract: Constructing the frozen manifold for entangled bands requires balancing exact reproduction of the target bands with sufficient variational freedom to build a well-localized subspace from the broader Bloch pool. We present a workflow that systematically determines the energy ceiling for a target number of selected Wannier projections, freezing every Bloch state below this threshold across the sampled k-mesh. By measuring projectability, the spectral weight of each Bloch state projected onto the target localized basis, the workflow detects missing conduction channels and quantifies discrepancies between orbital character and energy-based freezing. In comparisons where we controlled the extent of the energy ceiling, freezing all sub-ceiling states is generally favored over projectability-based frozen states. Of the seven materials we tested, freezing all sub-ceiling states lowers the band error on four from between 11 meV and 1.2 eV to 18 meV or less, and matches the projectability-based choice to within about 2 meV on the remaining three. In each of the four, projectability-based frozen states give the lower spread, showing that spread alone cannot identify the better model. With the frozen states held fixed, the workflow minimizes the gauge-invariant spread, constructs the gauge from density-matrix columns on atomic orbitals, and passes an isolated set of bands to Wannier90 for localization. The workflow is implemented in two programs for seamless high-throughput Wannierization with WIEN2k (wien2wannier) and CRYSTAL (LCAO2Wannier). Using a single set of calibrated defaults, the CRYSTAL implementation with analytic overlaps produces models that reproduce the reference bands of five cells, from bulk h-BN in a joint valence-and-conduction model to a magnetic framework with 1424 orbitals. The WIEN2k implementation produces eight such models from seven calculations.
subjects: Materials Science (cond-mat.mtrl-sci) ; Other Condensed Matter (cond-mat.other); Computational Physics (physics.comp-ph)

title: Capturing Open Quantum System Dynamics with Compact Dressed Hamiltonians
abstract: We advance the compact dressed Hamiltonian (CDH) framework to simulate the dynamics of open quantum systems strongly coupled to structured bosonic environments. The CDH approach combines reaction-coordinate mapping with a polaron transformation, incorporating strong system-environment hybridization into a dressed representation before truncating the collective bosonic mode. As a result of this truncation, dynamical features are captured with substantially fewer states than in the original representation. The residual environment is treated using a weak-coupling Markovian quantum master equation. We benchmark the method for spin-boson-type models including a single spin, coupled spins, and spin ensembles, considering both resonant and off-resonant regimes and weak to strong system-bath coupling. Comparisons with hierarchical equations of motion and converged reaction-coordinate calculations demonstrate that the CDH representation systematically approaches the reference dynamics with a compact Hilbert space, accurately reproducing oscillation frequencies, relaxation behavior, and long-time populations over a broad parameter regime. The method further captures cooperative phenomena, including bath-mediated interactions, synchronization between spins, and signatures for collective emission. Beyond efficient time propagation, the CDH framework provides direct access to the spectrum and eigenmodes of the Liouvillian. We demonstrate that slow dynamical modes converge rapidly in the CDH representation, enabling identification of relaxation timescales without fitting time-dependent observables. As a whole, the CDH framework provides an efficient and physical description of strongly coupled open quantum-system dynamics.
subjects: Quantum Physics (quant-ph) ; Mesoscale and Nanoscale Physics (cond-mat.mes-hall)

title: Floquet ground state order
abstract: Clean, interacting, periodically driven systems are believed to thermalize to featureless, infinite-temperature states that preclude the formation of stable ordered states. Here, we show stable quantum order, distinct from prethermal order, and its phase transitions in the ground state of the average-energy operator. Decomposing the time evolution into geometric and average-energy dynamics, we apply Geometric Floquet theory to identify the Floquet ground state. We derive a general variational principle to compute the Floquet ground state in large interacting periodically driven systems, and use it to develop a matrix product state algorithm. In driven nonintegrable chains of more than 100 interacting spins, our numerical simulations exhibit a gapped, area-law entangled Floquet ground state in extended parameter regimes; the ground-state manifold can support both dressed equilibrium order (e.g., Floquet antiferromagnets) and inherently nonequilibrium order (e.g., ground-state time crystals). This quantum order is protected by a finite average-energy gap, which closes at phase transition points upon changing model parameters. We decompose Floquet phases of matter into their equilibrium and nonequilibrium elements: whereas the Floquet ground state at any fixed time is a representative of an equilibrium phase of matter, the nonequilibrium content is entirely produced by the drive holonomy and is geometric. Finally, we identify quasilocal counterdiabatic driving as a mechanism for the stability against heating of gapped Floquet ground states in nonintegrable quantum systems, and argue why Floquet ground states evade the Eigenstate Thermalization Hypothesis. Our work enables the study of interacting nonequilibrium matter deep into the many-body regime, and lays the foundations for the engineering of strongly correlated ordered quantum states.
subjects: Quantum Physics (quant-ph) ; Other Condensed Matter (cond-mat.other); Quantum Gases (cond-mat.quant-gas); Statistical Mechanics (cond-mat.stat-mech); Strongly Correlated Electrons (cond-mat.str-el)

title: Observable-Level Framework for Finite-Key Security in Coherent-One-Way Quantum Key Distribution
abstract: Practical security analysis of Coherent-One-Way (COW) quantum key distribution requires optical-device modeling, finite experimental statistics, and security inference to be treated consistently without conflating assumptions. We present a modular observable-level simulation framework organized through the pipeline {\theta}_phys -> p -> O -> S_j(O), in which physical source, channel, receiver, and detector parameters determine detector-resolved event probabilities, a finite-block layer applies an effective dead-time treatment and generates aggregate detector counts, and interchangeable security evaluators act on the same observable record. The framework is verified against analytical optical, virtual-state, and finite-key relations and evaluated against reported experimental COW-QKD operating points. The Kato finite-key calculation reproduces the refined experimentally reported secure-key rates most closely at intermediate distances, with deviations of -1.5% at 50 km and -10.3% at 75 km. Monitoring bright-port decoy counts agree within 0.9-2.4%, while remaining distance-dependent dark-port residual identifies the principal model-sensitive observable of the present physical description. Applying Kato and Azuma-Hoeffding concentration treatments to identical detector records isolates the effect of finite-key statistical inference and shows substantially tighter Kato phase-error bounds for rare-event monitoring records studied here. Holding the Kato evaluator fixed, joint optimization of coherent-state mean photon number mu and receiver splitting fraction t_B increases model-predicted secure-key rate by 7.4-20.2% relative to optimization of mu alone with t_B = 0.3. The framework therefore provides a common computational interface for experimental reproduction, controlled security-model comparison, model-based protocol optimization, and modular adversarial stress testing in COW-QKD.
comments: Main Article: 9 Pages with 4 Figures. Supplemental Material: 7 Pages with 6 Figures

title: Microscopically informed self-consistent multi-resolvent closure for dense many-body spectra
abstract: The exact multi-resolvent hierarchy of dense many-body spectra encodes higher-order spectral-weight correlations, but closing it predictively for interacting Hamiltonians remains a challenge. We introduce the multi-resolvent self-consistency (MRSC) equations, which separate an exact algebraic hierarchy from an approximate finite-parameter closure. The exact Feshbach geometric identity organizes r-resolvent cumulants into a ladder over irreducible vertices Gamma^(r), and the projected hierarchy expresses those vertices as functionals of the cumulants. The closure works in finite parameters: a connectivity basis organizes a general Hamiltonian's seed into class amplitudes, and a causal r-fold Stieltjes representation with a moment-field identity reduce moment matching to a finite-dimensional problem closed at a predictive fixed point. On the free-fermion benchmark the tested exact identities are reproduced and the Faddeeva closure is recovered at r=1. In a blind test on the interacting Ising chain, with the exact two-resolvent data withheld, the Hamiltonian-derived closure predicts the tested probes to 0.35%-0.97%. At the observable level the exact two-resolvent sector supplies a sign-correct, energy-resolved correction to the single-resolvent baseline for the off-diagonal eigenstate-thermalization-hypothesis (ETH) variance, of order one relative to it. Closure errors organize hierarchically: a level-by-level deficit decomposition, anchor measurements of the isolatable terms, and an explicit propagation bound. The same moments further yield a diagnostic chain for the window conditions of local rotational invariance -- an exact drift-kernel identity, a proven single-state identifiability boundary, and a transferability census over couplings and realizations -- a finite-order framework, not a proof of universal emergence.

title: Sparse block encoding with low subnormalisation for quantum linear solvers on unstructured meshes
abstract: Unstructured meshes are widely used in modelling and simulation in Computational Fluid Dynamics (CFD) due to their geometric flexibility. However, they require an efficient block encoding circuit describing the system. Here, we present a new block encoding methodology for unstructured mesh solvers based on decomposing the system matrix into a sum of 1-sparse matrices. This block encoding is engineered to reduce subnormalisation even in the absence of structure by hiding the contribution of large matrix elements behind others. We investigate three methods of 1-sparse decomposition. Our circuit constructions can optionally take advantage of limited matrix bandwidth and repeated values. For example we consider digitisation (reduced precision), where the number of multiplexed rotation gates is equal to the number of non-unique matrix entries. We evaluate our methodologies using 2D and 3D CFD matrices for unstructured aerofoil meshes, structured cavity, and duct meshes, with and without matrix preconditioning. Our results show that we are able to achieve a block encoding with a near constant subnormalisation factor as the number of matrix preconditioning infill levels increases. This significantly reduces the subnormalised condition number and, in one case, reduces the degree of the QSP polynomial approximation to $1/x$ by 100,000. Reduced precision digitisation is shown to become more effective as the number of preconditioning infill levels is increased and, in one case, reduces the number of multiplexed rotations from 2,785,576 to 546 whilst maintaining an infidelity of $2.6\times10^{-5}$ relative to the classical solution. The effect of digitisation on QSVT solutions is demonstrated using 2D and 3D unstructured mesh aerofoil cases. Due to its flexibility and automatic applicability, we believe our 1-sparse decomposition block encoding can offer benefits to other quantum applications.

title: Fate of Discrete Time Crystals in Finite-Size Cavity QED Systems
abstract: It has been shown that Discrete Time Crystal (DTC) behavior may arise in the periodically driven, open Dicke model in the thermodynamic limit ($N \rightarrow \infty$). In this work, we demonstrate that finite $N$ non-mean-field fluctuations in this model can lead to decay rates and amplitudes of transient DTCs that display a non-trivial non-monotonic behavior with an increasing number of atoms. We show that the second-order cumulant expansion fails to capture the finite-size dynamics, while a stochastic version of the Truncated Wigner Approximation (TWA) is remarkably accurate, particularly in the large atom ensemble limit. Using the TWA and the Monte Carlo Wave Function (MCWF) approach, we identify three distinct dynamical regimes of transient DTC behavior in the finite-size Dicke model. We outline the mechanism behind the non-monotonic finite size dynamical decay of DTC order and discuss the implications for experiments performed on finite-sized atomic assemblies.
subjects: Quantum Physics (quant-ph) ; Quantum Gases (cond-mat.quant-gas); Atomic Physics (physics.atom-ph)

title: Microscopic Bipartition and Macroscopic Symmetry in a Rényi Entanglement Ensemble
abstract: Universal information extracted from entanglement at a critical point is commonly associated with the long-distance properties of the bulk state, while microscopic details of a lattice bipartition are expected to be washed out under coarse graining. Counterintuitively, we show directly that such microscopic information can survive in the statistical ensemble that determines the second Rényi entropy and obviously change the physics there. Using quantum Monte Carlo simulations of the square-lattice $J$-$Q_3$ model at the Néel--valence-bond-solid (VBS) transition, we measure magnetic and dimer order parameters in the Rényi-2 ensemble. For a standard axis-aligned bipartition, the VBS component perpendicular to the entanglement boundary remains finite in the thermodynamic extrapolation and is inequivalent to the parallel component, while the Néel order vanishes. For a $45^\circ$ tilted bipartition, in contrast, the two VBS components remain equivalent within numerical accuracy. We interpret this contrast in terms of the Rényi twist defect: the two bipartitions have the same bulk theory but realize different microscopic defect symmetries. Our results demonstrate that lattice information invisible to the bulk continuum theory alone can remain active in the long-distance Rényi ensemble, providing a microscopic explanation for the strong bipartition dependence previously observed in entanglement studies of deconfined criticality.

title: Quantum Fluctuations and Wigner Dynamics of a Carbon Nanotube Oscillator Driven by an Atomic Force Microscope
abstract: Suspended carbon nanotubes provide a useful platform for studying controlled nanomechanical motion in regimes where environmental fluctuations, memory effects, and quantum coherence can all influence the dynamics. We model the fundamental flexural mode of a carbon nanotube driven by an atomic force microscope as a harmonic quantum Brownian oscillator subject to a prescribed classical force and coupled linearly to a thermal environment. Starting from the generalized Langevin equation, we formulate the reduced dynamics directly in phase space, where the Wigner function evolves through a Gaussian propagator determined by dissipative linear transport, a deterministic force-induced displacement, and bath-induced fluctuations. For a Drude memory kernel, the retarded response is expressed through the three roots of a characteristic cubic equation. In the classical-noise limit, the three independent entries of the finite-time covariance matrix reduce to explicit finite sums over these response poles, eliminating numerical double-time covariance integration. We extend the construction to the full quantum fluctuation spectrum, obtaining a thermal frequency series representation that retains zero-point and low-temperature fluctuations. For an initial two-packet superposition, we examine interference attenuation and the integrated negative part of the Wigner function, which provides a phase space measure of nonclassicality. These results provide an explicit analytical framework for finite-memory quantum Brownian motion of bound oscillators and a tractable phase space description of driven carbon nanotube dynamics relevant to future quantum state preparation and quantum tomography experiments.
subjects: Quantum Physics (quant-ph) ; Mesoscale and Nanoscale Physics (cond-mat.mes-hall); Mathematical Physics (math-ph)

title: Dynamics of two bosons with density-assisted tunnelling in a one-dimensional tilted lattice
abstract: We investigate the dynamics of two bosons in a tilted one-dimensional optical lattice with both standard and density-assisted tunnelling. The relative sign of the two tunnelling processes strongly affects the Bloch dynamics, leading to distinct reinforcing and competing regimes. We examine how the tunnelling processes generate correlations and find that, in the absence of onsite interactions, the early-time entanglement growth follows the same scaling with the density-assisted tunnelling amplitude. Finite onsite interaction changes this picture by breaking the symmetry between the reinforcing and competing regimes and enhancing the correlation differently in two regimes. This shows how the interplay between the two tunnelling mechanisms can change dyanmics and entanglement in a controlled few-body setting. Particularly, at equal tunnelling amplitudes, the doublon and singlon sectors decouple completely for arbitrary onsite interaction, lattice tilting, and initial state.

title: Intrinsic Curvature Controls Spontaneous Entanglement of Elastic Rods
abstract: We report results from an experimental investigation on the role of intrinsic curvature in the spontaneous entanglement of elastic rods subjected to controlled tumbling. We examine two distinct entanglement mechanisms, knotting and locking, in a statistical ensemble of straight and helical rods with varying arc length and natural curvature. Our primary finding is that natural curvature exerts a dominant, non-monotonic influence on knotting, with a critical curvature that suppresses knot formation and significantly reduces the probability of knotting relative to equivalent straight rods. In contrast, locking is largely insensitive to curvature and scales primarily with rod length. These results, obtained for the macroscopic experimental system studied here, identify geometric parameters that govern distinct entanglement modes in tumbled elastic rods and may inform entanglement processes in microscopic filamentary systems such as DNA.

title: Cumulative locality governs collective quantum charging
abstract: Quantum batteries can outperform their classical counterparts through collective quantum effects, yet the conditions enabling such advantage remain unclear. Using a generic class of free-fermionic chargers we prove that global operators are insufficient for scalable superextensive charging and that a cumulative hierarchy of many-body operators is required, with the structure of the battery determining the degree of advantage. This is obtained by relating the charging power to the norm of the commutator between the battery and charger Hamiltonians and deriving an upper bound only capturing noncommuting terms. Moreover, we revisit the concept of participation number and propose an effective definition that accounts for the relative strength of the contributing terms, correlating it with the charging power scaling. Not limited to quadratic Hamiltonians, our results establish cumulative locality as a key resource for quantum charging advantage.
subjects: Quantum Physics (quant-ph) ; Statistical Mechanics (cond-mat.stat-mech); Strongly Correlated Electrons (cond-mat.str-el); Chaotic Dynamics (nlin.CD)
comments: Main text: 7 pages, 5 figures. Supplementary Information: 16 pages, 4 figures

title: Complete Modified Logarithmic Sobolev Inequalities for one-dimensional quantum Spin Chain
abstract: We prove a complete modified logarithmic Sobolev inequality with a system-size-independent constant for Chen--Kastoryano--Gilyén Gibbs samplers on one-dimensional spin chain at every fixed positive temperature. The result holds for Hamiltonians with bounded finite-range interactions, including noncommuting and spatially nonuniform interactions. It yields trace and diamond mixing times of order $O(\log N+\log(1/\epsilon))$. The proof establishes complete spatial entropy factorization and absorbs quasi-local errors as conditional relative entropy at the original joint state and reference. The static estimate also yields a system-size-independent CMLSI for the single-site Petz heat-bath and regularised heat-bath dynamics.

title: Chaos and scrambling in anisotropic Dicke and Rabi models
abstract: Identifying the quantum signatures of classical chaos remains a central question in quantum physics, and quantum scrambling provides a new perspective on this correspondence. We study two distinct limits of the same model to examine how the correspondence between chaos and scrambling changes across different regimes. The thermodynamic-limit anisotropic Dicke model exhibits a close correspondence between chaos and scrambling, whereas this correspondence breaks down in the large-frequency-ratio limit of the anisotropic Rabi model (ARM). The contrasting chaotic behavior in the two limits originates from the different numbers of classical degrees of freedom, whereas their similar scrambling behavior stems from eigenstate delocalization. This implies that, in the large-frequency-ratio limit, eigenstate delocalization alone is insufficient to qualify the ARM as a classically chaotic model. This finding suggests that identifying chaos in quantum systems requires jointly considering the classical degrees of freedom and eigenstate delocalization.

title: Scrambling Separates Superradiance from Quantum Chaos
abstract: Early studies on the Dicke model linked superradiance to quantum chaos, whereas later anisotropic Dicke and Rabi studies reached apparently conflicting conclusions. We resolve this tension by distinguishing global chaos from local instability. Along the isotropic Dicke path, a sweep at fixed low excitation energy crosses both the superradiant boundary and a nearby chaotic window, explaining the reported correlation. However, the anisotropic Dicke model can be chaotic in the normal phase and regular in the superradiant phase, making superradiance neither necessary nor sufficient for global chaos. A fidelity out-of-time-order correlator (FOTOC), in contrast, probes the local stability of the stationary point selected by the initial wave packet. The superradiant transition destabilizes the origin, whereas a change in anisotropy can restore its stability and create displaced saddles. Wave packets centered at these saddles exhibit exponential FOTOC growth even on a classically regular Dicke energy shell with Poisson statistics. This local sensitivity also enables quantitative spectroscopy: combined with the topology of stationary points and local density of states relations, FOTOC dynamics reconstructs the absolute amplitudes of spectral singularities in both models without fitting the density of states.
comments: 15 pages (6-page main text and 9-page Supplemental Material), 9 figures, 4 tables

title: Hidden parabolic subgroups of $\mathrm{GL}_n$ over finite chain rings
abstract: We give a bounded-error quantum polynomial-time algorithm for finding hidden parabolic subgroups of $\mathrm{GL}_n(R)$ over any effectively presented finite chain ring $R$. We call auxiliary group elements or subgroups used to extract information through oracle queries \emph{probes}. For chain length at least two, elementary abelian socle probes first recover the complete flag modulo the maximal ideal. When the residue field has size $q\ge3$, we reconstruct the flag recursively, lifting rank-one terminal members one digit at a time. The intermediate digits reduce to abelian hidden subgroup problems, while the final digit is a finite-field multiple-shift problem solved using learning from subset and Fourier sampling. For $q=2$, where distinct flags can have the same stabilizer, we instead lift the conjugate parabolic subgroup through the congruence filtration. A final linear system determines it modulo normalizer directions. The algorithm outputs generators with probability at least $1-\epsilon$ in time $\mathrm{poly}(n,\log|R|,\log(1/\epsilon))$. Consequences include $\mathrm{GL}_n(\mathbb{Z}/N\mathbb{Z})$ for every $N\ge2$ and, with an explicit maximal-order presentation, $\mathrm{GL}_n(\mathcal{O_K}/N\mathcal{O_K})$ for number fields $K$.

title: Dimension-free marginal inequalities for pure three-party states
abstract: The quantum marginal problem, concerned with the compatibility of local and global properties of a multipartite quantum system, is arguably one of the fundamental questions in quantum theory. In this article we introduce a novel family of inequalities bounding the allowed local spectra of a pure tripartite state. The number of inequalities in this family grows with the dimension of the system. Most importantly, the inequalities hold for arbitrary dimensions. For equal local dimension at most 4, they generate the complete set of eigenvalue inequalities.
comments: 6 pages. This is a preliminary version. I would have liked to spend more time on the presentation of the results, but in this fast-moving times I prefer to upload a first version. Comments welcome

title: Measurement incompatibility in Bayesian quantum estimation beyond quadratic loss
abstract: In single-shot Bayesian multiparameter quantum estimation, measurement incompatibility can increase the minimum joint quadratic loss by at most a factor of two relative to the bound obtained by optimising each parameter separately. Using the generalised Barnum--Knill inequality, we establish the same bound for a wider class of additive losses generated by positive score functions, showing that this limitation extends beyond the standard quadratic setting. To illustrate this result, we consider a broad family of periodic losses, including the sine loss sometimes employed in interferometry, and derive the corresponding incompatibility bound for Bayesian multiphase estimation with arbitrary prior knowledge. We further extend the framework to unbounded losses, such as absolute losses; this also recovers the case of quadratic losses.

title: A $q$-Inspired Radial Quantum Kinematics
abstract: We study how the one-dimensional deformation suggested by nonadditive $q$-calculus can be extended to a rotationally covariant quantum model and what observable consequences follow from this extension. We choose a radial extension about a distinguished center in which only the radial derivative is deformed, while tangential derivatives retain their ordinary form. Within this model, we construct self-adjoint frame-momentum operators and derive a rotationally invariant uncertainty bound with a correction proportional to the mean distance from the center. We then adopt a non-negative kinetic Hamiltonian built from these momenta and derive the leading harmonic-oscillator energy shifts for weak deformation. The energy corrections split the levels with different orbital angular momenta that are degenerate in the undeformed oscillator, while preserving the degeneracy associated with rotational symmetry.

title: Phase shifts and fluctuations from motional, relativistic, and dark-matter effects in ion-trap clocks
abstract: Ions possess both center-of-mass motion and internal states, rendering trapped-ion optical clocks susceptible to perturbations of both degrees of freedom, which results in systematic shifts and fluctuations with motional and relativistic origins. We develop a quantum theory that connects these effects to filter functions determined by the employed pulse sequences and show how the interrogation can be tailored to suppress or enhance specific perturbations. Our treatment includes laser frequency noise and motional effects such as recoil and Doppler shifts, micromotion and excess micromotion, as well as state-dependent trap imperfections and accelerations, e.g., caused by Stark shifts. We further account for relativistic effects including time dilation and the mass defect, and show how the same framework can be applied to hypothetical dark-matter signals. By considering ensemble-averaged phases and their variances, we characterize both systematic shifts and fluctuations, while asynchronous operation relative to the Paul-trap drive allows motional fluctuations to average down between runs. Our results provide a unified framework for characterizing and controlling the systematic and statistical contributions that determine the trueness and precision of trapped-ion optical clocks.
subjects: Quantum Physics (quant-ph) ; Atomic and Molecular Clusters (physics.atm-clus)

title: Cooling more while dissipating less: anomalous tradeoffs from thermodynamic geometry
abstract: We show that, starting from the same state, optimal driving can sometimes reach a colder (or hotter) target in the same amount of time while dissipating less energy, or equivalently dissipate the same amount of energy in a shorter time. We study this counterintuitive phenomenon in the slow-driving regime of an open quantum system, where we name it Near-Equilibrium Anomalous Tradeoff (NEAT). We establish necessary conditions for its occurrence and show its underlying geometric origin. While NEAT is reminiscent of the well-known Mpemba effect, the two phenomena are distinct in general. We demonstrate NEAT in an exactly solvable qutrit model, as well as for d-dimensional birth-death dynamics with independently controlled energy levels. Finally, we show how NEAT can improve the performance of Carnot engines.

title: Local-Channel Stability of Classical $\mathbb Z_2$ Lattice Gauge Models
abstract: We establish sufficient conditions for two-way local quantum-channel stability in classical $\mathbb Z_2$ lattice gauge models with spins on $m$-dimensional cells of a $d$-dimensional lattice. Each interaction multiplies the spins on the boundary of an $(m+1)$-cell. This family, defined on the full spin Hilbert space without a Gauss-law constraint, includes the Ising model at $m=0$ and the magnetic sector of the toric code at $m=1$. The low-temperature proof combines two ingredients: locally indistinguishable flat sectors and extended magnetic defects of dimension $d-m-1$. For $1\le m\le d-2$, sufficiently weak local classical perturbations at sufficiently low positive temperature preserve equivalence to the canonical flat ensemble. No internal or gauge symmetry is required of the perturbation. For weak noncommuting perturbations, we prove the same conclusion in a smaller sufficient window by reducing the diagonal probabilities to a weak classical interaction and recovering the coherences with a local channel. The conversion channels use product ancillary inputs, have polylogarithmic causal radius, and achieve any prescribed inverse-power whole-system trace-norm error. Sufficiently high-temperature states are instead two-way equivalent to a product state. Independent finite-dimensional onsite systems can be included with weak local couplings. An optimized covariance between two distant neighborhoods of parallel $m$-tori is nonincreasing under one-way local conversion and invariant under two-way conversion. Its values $\mathcal F_m=1$ and $0$ distinguish the proved low- and high-temperature domains without a protecting symmetry. These sufficient domains do not determine the full phase diagram.
subjects: Quantum Physics (quant-ph) ; Other Condensed Matter (cond-mat.other); Statistical Mechanics (cond-mat.stat-mech); Strongly Correlated Electrons (cond-mat.str-el)

title: Fates of Exact Finite-$N$ First-Order Transitions: Coherent Suppression versus Spectral-Collapse Termination
abstract: Symmetry-protected ground-state crossings can produce exact first-order transitions (FOTs) even at finite $N$, in contrast to continuous transitions governed by soft-mode criticality. We establish exact Juddian ground-state crossings for arbitrary finite $N$ in the one- and two-photon anisotropic Dicke models and identify a common two-channel structure: the eigenvalues of the coupling matrix set the local normal-state instability thresholds, whereas its determinant fixes the exact crossing. Despite this common structure, the resulting FOTs have distinct fates determined by the bosonic response. In the one-photon model, the overlap between coherent Juddian branches vanishes in the thermodynamic or infinite frequency-ratio limits, asymptotically suppressing the FOT cusp. In the two-photon model, squeezed Juddian states lose normalizability at spectral collapse, thereby terminating the physical FOT line at finite $N$. Although the cusp strength tends to zero as the endpoint is approached, the terminating FOT retains a collective spectral signature: the different-parity gap is predicted to close with an $N$-dependent exponent $\mu_N=(2N+3)/4$, one greater than the cusp termination exponent. By contrast, the same-parity soft mode retains $N$-independent square-root scaling and governs the critical response. Thus spectral collapse can terminate an exact finite-$N$ FOT while preserving its collective imprint in the parity-resolved spectrum.

title: Axion detection in the non-Markovian noise
author_note: Showing the first 3 and last 3 of 7 authors
abstract: The detection of axion dark matter poses a significant challenge due to its exceptionally weak coupling to standard-model particles. Here we develop a noise-tolerant quantum-metrology scheme based on coupled $^{129}$Xe spin ensembles to search for such weakly interacting particles. Within an experimentally accessible parameter regime, our scheme achieves an ideal exclusion limit on the axion coupling constant that is several orders of magnitude more stringent than that of conventional detection methods. We further investigate the performance of our scheme under dissipative noise and find that its robustness is fundamentally governed by the energy-spectrum structure of the composite spin-environment system. Remarkably, when a bound state emerges in the spectrum, the exclusion limit asymptotically recovers its ideal value in the non-Markovian dynamics, whereas under the Markovian approximation the limit deteriorates significantly due to noise. Our results establish a universal mechanism for noise-resilient exploration of beyond-standard-model physics, which can be practically implemented by engineering bound-state formation via tuning the Larmor frequency of the spin ensembles.
subjects: Quantum Physics (quant-ph) ; Cosmology and Nongalactic Astrophysics (astro-ph.CO)

title: Stabilizer Rényi moments beyond entanglement
abstract: Stabilizer Rényi moments depend on a choice of operator basis and need not be determined by entanglement spectra. In this paper, we study their spatial decay in critical quantum chains described by two-dimensional conformal field theories. We derive an exact entanglement baseline for reductions of pure stabilizer states and a symmetry selection rule for the charged contribution at fixed support. An exact Ising example shows that an on-site rotation changes the full decay exponent while preserving every subsystem entanglement spectrum. For growing Ising intervals at index two, we obtain an exact Pfaffian representation and compare the charged amplitude with a candidate conformal boundary calculation. The data support this prediction, but its identification with the lattice limit still requires endpoint matching and control of the order of limits.
subjects: Quantum Physics (quant-ph) ; Strongly Correlated Electrons (cond-mat.str-el); High Energy Physics - Theory (hep-th)

title: Low-nonlinearity advantage of hollow-core fiber for wavelength multiplexing of quantum entanglement and classical DWDM signals
author_note: Showing the first 3 and last 3 of 10 authors
abstract: Coexistence of classical and quantum light in optical fiber is a key requirement for scalable quantum networks. However, it is fundamentally limited by nonlinear crosstalk from intense classical signals. Hollow-core fiber (HCF), with its intrinsically low optical nonlinearity, offers a promising solution. Here, we experimentally demonstrate the coexistence of polarization-entangled photons with dense wavelength-division multiplexed (DWDM) classical signals with a total launch power of 11.2 dBm, and perform a direct comparison between equal-length single-mode fiber (SMF) and photonic-bandgap-based HCF deployed in a campus network. We observe that HCF suppresses background noise by approximately two orders of magnitude compared to SMF, while preserving high-fidelity entanglement distribution. Our results provide clear experimental evidence of the advantage of HCF and establish its potential as a transmission medium.

title: Choi-Jamiołkowski isomorphism(s) and channel/state duality, naturally!
abstract: Provided a maximally entangled state vector in ${\mathcal{H}}\otimes{\mathcal{H}}$, the Choi-Jamiolkowski isomorphism of quantum information theory (or channel/state duality) produces a mapping of ${\mathsf CP}({\mathcal{H}},{\mathcal{K}})$ (completely positive maps of density operators on ${\mathcal{H}}$ tothose on ${\mathcal{K}}$) onto the density operators on ${\mathcal{K}}\otimes{\mathcal{H}}$, which extends to a unitary map. Here, ${\mathcal{H}}$ and ${\mathcal{K}}$ are {finite-dimensional} Hilbert this http URL nature of this construction, the form of the associated formulas, and the possibility of versions which do not require an entangled vector seed, are illuminated from the perspective of {naturality}, in the sense of Eilenberg and this http URL is a unique such correspondence (``Choi map'') natural in both ${\mathcal{H}}$ and ${\mathcal{K}}$ which produces density operators on either ${\mathsf L}({\mathcal{H}},{\mathcal{K}})$ (Hilbert-Schmidt inner product) or ${\mathcal{K}}\otimes{\mathcal{H}}^*$ instead of ${\mathcal{K}}\otimes{\mathcal{H}}$. In particular, no entangled state input is required. There are no such binatural maps carried on ${\mathcal{K}}\otimes{\mathcal{H}}$, but those natural in only ${\mathcal{K}}$ are canonically associated with unitary maps ${\mathcal{H}}\rightarrow{\mathcal{H}}^*$ and derive from the binatural maps. The construction recovers the standard Choi-Jamiolkowski formulae and shows how they express naturality.

title: Assignment maps for arbitrary reduced quantum dynamics
abstract: Given an open quantum system $S$ with environment $E$, we establish a one-to-one correspondence between completely positive trace-preserving (CPTP) maps from $S$ to $E$ and assignment maps initializing the composite system $SE$ in a possibly correlated state prior to unitary evolution. We show that every possible joint state $\rho_{SE}$ can be realized by such assignment maps, which are inherently Hermiticity-preserving and trace-preserving (HPTP). While these maps sacrifice global positivity, we derive a simple necessary and sufficient condition for any local state of $S$ to belong to their domain of validity. Furthermore, we prove that the geometry of this domain is governed by the joint state assigned to the maximally mixed input, ensuring that a non-zero volume of admissible local states can readily coexist with initial system-environment entanglement. Finally, we provide an operational protocol for witnessing such limits of validity.

title: Comparative Optical Spectroscopy of Er$^{3+}$, Tm$^{3+}$, and Eu$^{3+}$ Molecular Complexes at Cryogenic Temperature
author_note: Showing the first 3 and last 3 of 7 authors
abstract: Rare-earth molecular complexes are attracting increasing interest for quantum information applications because of their structural flexibility and chemical tunability. Here, we compare the cryogenic optical properties of Er$^{3+}$, Tm$^{3+}$, and Eu$^{3+}$ complexes in the same ligand environment. Optical spectroscopy shows differing behavior across the three systems: spectral hole burning is observed in the Eu$^{3+}$ complex, whereas no measurable hole is detected in the Er$^{3+}$ and Tm$^{3+}$ complexes. We measure laser-induced local heating and rethermalization in the Er$^{3+}$ and Tm$^{3+}$ powder-like samples, observing strong local heating and slow thermal relaxation in the cold-plate cryostat. The recovery occurs over several seconds and, for some Er$^{3+}$ excitation conditions, extends over tens of seconds. The comparison across the three ions nevertheless suggests that heating alone is unlikely to account for the full contrast. Rather, the different behaviors of Eu$^{3+}$, Tm$^{3+}$, and Er$^{3+}$ point to ion-dependent relaxation and decoherence processes associated with their electronic level structure and coupling to the molecular environment. Temperature-dependent linewidth and line-shift measurements are further consistent with phonon-mediated broadening through coupling to crystal-field levels.

title: The next phase of quantum energy science: from mechanisms to applications
abstract: A growing research community spanning quantum batteries, molecular and excitonic energy transport, polaritonics, quantum materials and nuclear control has begun to describe its work in terms of quantum energy or quantum energy science. What connects these otherwise disparate efforts is the deliberate use of quantum states, couplings, collective effects and engineered environments to control energetic states and pathways. A key difference from quantum information science is that the complete quantum state does not always need to be preserved; engineered dissipation or dephasing can even improve the desired outcome. We organize this emerging domain through a framework that connects mechanisms, functions, capabilities, and applications. We identify five elementary functions (Excite, Hold, Release, Transfer, and Transform) and examine the mechanisms that implement them. The same functions recur from the molecular to the nuclear scale, although their relative implementation difficulty can differ sharply. Moving toward technology, we highlight three engineering capabilities (Storage, Routing, and Conversion) through the performance metrics that matter for their applications. Stretch scenarios illustrate what performance targets could make these capabilities technologically consequential.

title: Optimal Approximate Quantum Conversion from a Taut-String Principle in Majorization-Based Resource Theories
abstract: Optimal approximate state conversion is a fundamental task in quantum resource theories, yet existing solutions are largely tailored to specific distinguishability measures and resource theories. We show that every optimal approximate-conversion problem in the three paradigmatic majorization-based quantum resource theories of non-uniformity, bipartite pure-state entanglement, and pure-state coherence reduces exactly to one of only four elementary taut-string constructions. This holds for problems generated by Schur-convex spectral distances and by a broad family of quantum divergences satisfying a natural reduction property with respect to the corresponding equivalence group. The resulting framework encompasses a broad class of physically relevant distinguishability measures, including the trace distance, all unitarily invariant norms, quantum relative entropy, maximal quantum $f$-divergences, and the $\alpha$-$z$ Rényi relative entropies. The increment vector of the corresponding taut string completely determines both the optimal approximation error and a canonical optimal state. Our results establish a common geometric framework for approximate quantum resource conversion, revealing that a broad class of seemingly different optimization problems is governed by the same taut-string geometric principle.

title: Concurrent Entanglement Purification Scheduling in Dynamic Quantum Networks
abstract: Quantum networks must deliver end-to-end entanglement whose fidelity meets application requirements, which typically requires entanglement purification along multi-hop paths. Existing scheduling approaches either purify at the link level or optimize end-to-end fidelity for a static set of requests, and do not capture concurrent requests competing for network resources over time. This paper studies concurrent entanglement purification scheduling in a time-slotted quantum network with heterogeneous links, in which requests compete for link capacity and quantum memories, and each request may be served by multiple parallel paths for increased reliability. We formulate a mixed-integer linear programming (MILP) scheduler that maximizes the number of scheduled requests, with max-min path allocation as a fairness criterion, and develop reinforcement learning (RL) schedulers based on DQN, PPO, and SAC, whose rewards balance request success against Bell-pair consumption. Simulations under varying network load, topologies and target fidelity thresholds show that the RL schedulers achieve the highest success rates, improving on MILP by up to 6% and on Progressive Filling and Greedy heuristics by 16.5% and 19.5% respectively, at the cost of higher Bell pair consumption and the deferral of a small fraction of requests. MILP, in contrast, achieves the highest fairness and the lowest Bell pair consumption in most scenarios.

title: Characterizing supersolid phase transitions in trapped quantum gases with tilted dipoles at finite temperature
abstract: Motivated by a recent experimental work $[\href{ https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.20327 }{\text{arXiv:} 2608.20327 }]$, we theoretically investigate the nature of phase transitions in a trapped dipolar quantum gas upon tuning the contact interaction strength and dipole orientation. Using extended Gross-Pitaevskii simulations including thermal and quantum effects, we map the phase diagram comprising unmodulated superfluids, triangular droplet arrays, and stripe states. We further characterize the order of the transitions separating them through imaginary-time hysteresis analysis. The unmodulated-to-modulated transition evolves from discontinuous to continuous with increasing dipole tilt before becoming discontinuous again at large tilts. The degree of continuity is further affected by particle number, temperature, and confinement. While continuous behavior generally correlates with the emergence of stripe states, this correspondence is not systematic, and finite-size effects also influence the continuity of the transition. The triangular-to-stripe transition is found to be discontinuous at small contact interaction strengths and becomes increasingly continuous upon approaching the unmodulated-to-modulated phase boundary. Our results reveal a tunable transition order in finite dipolar quantum gases and provide guidance for its experimental investigation.
subjects: Quantum Gases (cond-mat.quant-gas) ; Statistical Mechanics (cond-mat.stat-mech); Quantum Physics (quant-ph)

title: Multiscale Modeling of Zr Corrosion: Predicting Microstructures of Oxide Films
author_note: Showing the first 3 and last 3 of 8 authors
abstract: A first-principles-informed multiscale modeling approach is reported for oxide formation during corrosion of zirconium. The present simulations reproduce the columnar corrosion film microstructure and grain size distribution seen in micrographs of oxidized Zr surfaces. This structural feature emerges from a hexagonal ZrO layer adjacent to the $\alpha$-Zr/ZrO$_{2-x}$ interface, which is dynamically stabilized by continuous heterogeneous grain nucleation and grain boundary mass diffusion. This ZrO layer is identified as a significant oxygen diffusion barrier and a potential contributor to sub-parabolic pretransition corrosion kinetics. The simulations also reproduce the undulatory nature of the metal/oxide interface, leading to regions with tensile stress components capable of nucleating cracks, despite the overall state of compressive hydrostatic stress within the oxide film. First principles density functional theory (DFT) computations of fundamental ZrO$_x$ properties were combined with molecular dynamics simulations using a machine-learned potential based on a DFT training set to provide extensive input to an advanced phase field model for oxide formation and its microstructure, as implemented in the new MedeA PhaseField module. The phase field simulations reported herein incorporated computed stoichiometry-dependent thermochemical data, anisotropic elastic properties, interface energies, bulk and grain boundary mass transport processes, multiphase heterogeneous grain nucleation, and strain energy-dependent phase stabilities.
